answers_by_date.basis: Constitution Art. 21 (amparo, unchanged since 1980) let any person 'arrestado, detenido o preso con infracción' of the Constitution or laws, and anyone suffering 'cualquiera otra privación, perturbación o amenaza' to personal liberty, go to court. The court could order release or correct defects. DL 1.094 Art. 89 allowed a judicial reclamación to the Supreme Court against expulsion decrees. The Código Procesal Penal (Art. 95) was not yet in force anywhere: it was published Oct 2000 and in force from 16-12-2000 in two regions. No migrant-specific practice evidence was found for this period; the 2020 rating is carried forward.

Same constitutional amparo and DL 1.094 Art. 89. CPP Art. 95 ('amparo ante el juez de garantía' to examine legality and conditions) was in force in all regions except the Región Metropolitana, where it applied only from 16-06-2005. CAT 2004 concerns ill-treatment and overcrowding in general, not migrants' access to amparo; there is no migrant-specific evidence.

Constitution Art. 21, DL 1.094 Arts. 89-90 and CPP Art. 95 were in force nationwide. CPP Art. 132 was amended by Ley 20.074 (14-11-2005), which does not affect the review right. No migrant-specific practice found for c.2010.

Same provisions; none was amended in a way relevant to the indicator. Practice: in March 2013 the Santiago Court of Appeals, confirmed by the Supreme Court, granted amparo to 17 migrants held about two months in insalubrious, overcrowded conditions at Cuartel Borgoño pending expulsion. The court ordered their release and an investigation. This shows the remedy works, after delay.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: Constitution Art. 21 and DL 1.094 Arts. 84/89/90 were read on LeyChile with amendment markers: no change 2000-2020 (Art. 21 only CPR 1980; DL 1.094 only Ley 18.252/1983). The CPP entry-into-force schedule was read in Art. 484. The old Código de Procedimiento Penal amparo (in force for 2000/2005 in Santiago) was not read. Practice before 2013 is absent.
answers.notes: The protection answer relies on statutes and the Constitution, not on court rulings; the rulings are practice evidence only, read via press. The CPP's gradual entry into force (2000-2005) added an explicit 'conditions' review, but the constitutional amparo (Art. 21 inc. 3, 'cualquiera otra privación, perturbación o amenaza') already reached all three aspects under the starting coding's reading, so the answer is unchanged. Implementation for 2000/2005/2010 has no migrant-specific evidence (low confidence for those dates).

answers_by_date.basis: DL 1.094 Art. 84 requires expulsion 'por decreto supremo fundado' (tourists: Intendente resolution 'sin más trámite'). DS 597 Art. 176 limits deprivation of liberty to what is 'estrictamente necesarias'. Detention during the Art. 89 reclamación is automatic. No practice evidence for c.2000.
Same provisions; no amendment to DL 1.094 Arts. 81-90 or DS 597 Arts. 167-176 since 1983/1984. No migrant-specific practice evidence c.2005.

Same provisions. Ley 20.430 (refugees, 2010) did not alter expulsion-detention rules. DS 597 Art. 59 (asylum seekers detainable up to 15 days 'cuando existan fundados temores' of absconding) still appears in the text. No practice evidence c.2010.

Same provisions. Practice: the 2013 Cuartel Borgoño case shows about two months of detention of 17 migrants pending expulsion, found unlawful on amparo. This points to non-individualised, prolonged administrative detention.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

answers.sourcing_note: DL 1.094 version markers show no amendment of Arts. 81-90 between 1983 and its 2022 repeal. DS 597 was read in its last consolidated text, where Arts. 174 and 176 carry no amendment markers. Practice before 2013 is absent; the 2013/2018 evidence comes from press reports.
answers.starting_answer_concern: The 2020 answer cites Ley 21.325 Arts. 133-134, not in force until 12-02-2022. Its predecessor, DL 1.094, required a 'decreto supremo fundado' for the expulsion itself, but made detention automatic during the reclamación (Art. 89: 'permanecerá privado de su libertad'). It also allowed tourist expulsions 'sin más trámite' (Art. 84). Only the regulation (DS 597 Art. 176) limited deprivation of liberty to what is 'estrictamente necesarias'. A 'Yes' for an individualised detention determination in 2020 is therefore doubtful. The 2020 implementation 'Sometimes; Effectively Always' is not a permitted neighbouring pair.
answers.notes: The 2020 implementation could not be carried forward verbatim (not a valid option); 'Sometimes; Usually' is used for past dates on the strength of the 2013 Borgoño evidence. The CPP Art. 134 citation concerns criminal flagrancy detention, not immigration detention. The answer rests on statutes and regulation, not rulings.

answers_by_date.basis: Constitution Art. 19 No. 1 ('Se prohíbe la aplicación de todo apremio ilegítimo', for 'todas las personas') and Art. 5 inc. 2 (treaty rights). The UN Convention against Torture was promulgated by Decreto 808/1988, with reservations withdrawn in 1991 and on 23-12-1999. Penal Code Art. 150 A (Ley 19.567, 1998) punished 'tormentos o apremios ilegítimos, físicos o mentales'. No migrant-specific practice evidence; general evidence comes from CAT 2004.

Same provisions (Ley 20.050 of Aug 2005 did not touch Art. 19 No. 1). CAT 2004 noted 'continued ill-treatment of persons, in some cases amounting to torture' by Carabineros, PDI and Gendarmería, and an incomplete torture definition. This concerns detainees generally, not migrants.
Same provisions; Penal Code Art. 150 A in its 1998 text. No migrant-specific practice evidence found for c.2010.

Same provisions (150 A in 1998 text, read in the 2015 version). The US State Department's 2014 report notes reports of excessive force, abuse and degrading treatment by Carabineros, PDI and Gendarmería, and INDH concern over abuses against immigrants. Ley 20.968 (22-11-2016) later replaced 150 A and added 150 B-D, explicitly penalising CIDT.

answers.change_2000_2020: There have been right protections both in 2000 and 2020 and neither the right protection nor the implementation level of these protections has changed

After: a separate torture offence with the CAT-style definition, and Art. 150 D on 'apremios ilegítimos u otros tratos crueles, inhumanos o degradantes'. Both before and after, the answer is Yes.

answers.sourcing_note: The Penal Code was read in its 2015 version (Ley 19.567 text) and its current version (Ley 20.968). Constitution Art. 19 No. 1 and Decreto 808 notes were read on LeyChile. The American Convention promulgation decree was not read. Practice sources concern detainees generally, not migrants specifically; there is no source c.2000 or c.2010.
answers.notes: The protection answer rests on the Constitution (Art. 19 No. 1, applying to 'todas las personas' including migrants) and on the CAT incorporated via promulgation decree and Art. 5 inc. 2; the Penal Code reinforces it. No court ruling is relied on. Ley 21.325 Arts. 1, 3 and 13 postdate 2020 and are irrelevant to the past dates. Implementation evidence is about detainees and protesters generally (HRW 2020 covers the October 2019 protests, i.e. before the 2020 date); none is migrant-specific, hence low confidence.
